analysis.one_liner: Requires every employer to provide health coverage to employees and their families, with state plans covering the poor.
analysis.headline: The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee reported the bill favorably on November 20, 1989 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but it never received a floor vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every employer to enroll employees and their families in a health plan meeting federal minimum standards — hospital and physician care, tests, prenatal and well-baby care, and mental health benefits — with caps on deductibles, copays, and out-of-pocket costs, a ban on pre-existing condition exclusions, and a free-premium plan for low-wage workers. People without employer coverage would be phased into state-run programs starting with the poor. Employers that did not already offer coverage would have to buy plans from certified 'regional insurers' charging community-rated premiums, and small businesses whose compliance costs exceeded 5% of revenue could get a federal subsidy covering 75% of the excess.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without health coverage, their families, and people with pre-existing conditions would gain guaranteed access to a defined basic benefit package. Low-wage workers would be offered at least one plan with no employee premium. Poor and near-poor people without employer coverage would eventually be covered by state programs with no cost-sharing for the poor.

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must enroll each employee and the employee's family in a health benefit plan meeting federal minimum requirements, and employees cannot waive enrollment for themselves.

Plans must cover inpatient and outpatient hospital care, physician services, diagnostic and screening tests, prenatal and well-baby care, and mental health care (at least 45 inpatient days and 20 outpatient visits a year), with no limits on the amount, scope, or duration of core benefits.

Plans may not exclude or limit coverage for any pre-existing condition, must cap employee premiums at 20% of the plan's actuarial rate, cap deductibles ($250 individual/$500 family in the first year, indexed to inflation), cap copays and coinsurance at 20%, and cap annual out-of-pocket expenses at $3,000 for a family, indexed to inflation.

Employers must offer at least one plan with no employee premium to workers earning less than 125% of the minimum wage, and may not discriminate against applicants because they have a spouse or child who would need coverage.

States must phase in a program covering individuals under the poverty line starting in 1991, near-poverty individuals (up to 185% of poverty) by 1996, and everyone else not covered by an employer plan by 1999, with no premiums, deductibles, or cost-sharing for under-poverty individuals and federal payments to states for part of the cost.
Small employers whose compliance costs exceed 5% of gross revenues would be reimbursed for 75% of the excess.

New small employers and small employers changing insurers would buy coverage through certified regional insurers required to use community rating, meaning premiums could not be set based on age, gender, or health status.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost of enrolling workers and their families in plans, though employers can pass up to 20% of the premium cost to employees, and economists generally expect employer-mandate costs to show up partly in wages. Federal taxpayers subsidize small businesses and pay a share of state program costs. Health insurers gain millions of required customers but submit to certification, community rating, and decertification.

drawbacks.text: The employer mandate is a hidden tax on jobs and wages: employers must pay for coverage for anyone working 17.5 hours a week or more, and economists generally expect some of that cost to be borne by workers through slower wage growth or reduced hiring, especially for low-wage and part-time workers.
Employees can still be charged premiums up to 20% of the plan's cost, plus deductibles, copays, and coinsurance up to $3,000 a year for a family, so coverage is not free for most workers.

Coverage for people without employer-based coverage is phased in slowly: only the under-poverty population is guaranteed from 1991, near-poverty people must wait until 1996, and everyone else must wait until 1999.

The bill entrenches private insurers as the delivery channel: employers without coverage and small employers changing insurers must buy from certified regional insurers, and large employers with existing plans are carved out, so the private insurance system becomes the permanent mechanism for a near-universal public benefit.
Most routine preventive care other than prenatal and well-baby care is not required, and plan limits on prenatal and well-baby care are allowed under regulations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have extended guaranteed coverage to virtually the entire population, banned pre-existing condition exclusions, and capped out-of-pocket costs — benefits with few modern equivalents at the time. But it did so through an employer mandate whose costs would fall partly on wages and hiring, kept employee cost-sharing substantial, delayed universal state coverage until 1999, and locked private insurers in as the delivery system rather than creating a public alternative. It was a broad but insurer-centered design: large gains for the uninsured, significant costs for employers and taxpayers, and a permanent guaranteed market for the insurance industry.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it with an amendment and put it on the Senate's calendar of pending business, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Kennedy introduced the Basic Health Benefits for All Americans Act on April 12, 1989, with four Democratic cosponsors.

The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee held hearings in May and June 1989, requested comments from the Department of Health and Human Services and the Office of Management and Budget, and on July 12, 1989 ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On November 20, 1989 the committee reported the bill with an amendment, and Senate Republicans filed minority views in the committee report.

The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 409) — the list of bills awaiting floor action — but no senator ever moved for a vote, and the bill never reached the House.

The reported version dropped the individual right to sue for injunctive relief that appeared in the introduced bill and added a small business advisory committee, but kept the employer mandate, the regional insurer system, and the state coverage phase-in intact.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers avoided a mandate to cover employees and their families, and the uninsured — including people with pre-existing conditions — remained without guaranteed coverage. The Senate's broader 1991-92 health reform efforts also failed, so nothing replaced it until decades later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoided the mandate; the uninsured stayed uncovered

industries.note: The mandate makes private insurance the permanent channel for near-universal coverage: employers without plans, and small employers changing insurers, must buy from certified 'regional insurers,' guaranteeing the industry millions of customers. In exchange, insurers submit to federal certification, community rating (no premiums based on age, gender, or health), and possible decertification.

Every employer must pay to enroll employees and families in plans meeting federal standards, facing civil penalties up to 10% of total wages for noncompliance. Small businesses get a subsidy covering 75% of compliance costs above 5% of revenue, but the mandate is still a new cost.
Temporary workers are generally excluded, but those assigned 750 hours within six months count as employees who must be covered, adding costs for the staffing industry and coverage for those workers.

State and local governments must cover their employees or lose Public Health Service Act grants, contracts, loans, and loan guarantees, and must build state programs for the poor with federal matching funds.
